findings.F1: Inside the falling calm profile (255 grid cases over 3 days), the unusual 3-day move rises steadily across quintiles of the scaled 7-day return, from −2.48 % (t −1.87, 44 cases) in the lowest to +2.04 % (t 2.15, 43 cases) in the highest; bars with forecast > 0 average +1.24 % (t 1.96, 106 cases) against −1.37 % (t −2.14, 149 cases) for bars with forecast 0, so the tested idea's own variable carries the gradient in this data.
findings.F2: The close's place in its 20-day range does better than the scaled 7-day rise at a 5-day horizon: its top tercile gives +2.65 % (t 2.04, 43 cases on 31 days, Spearman 0.24), against +0.76 % (t 0.43) for the scaled 7-day rise's top tercile. But the two measures are correlated (Spearman 0.68), and among the 82 cases with a 7-day rise the range place adds nothing (Spearman 0.05, against 0.15 for the scaled rise), so it is the same effect measured another way.
findings.F3: The sharpest pattern found is on the short side: 7-day falls that close in the lowest third of their day's range are followed by −3.95 % over 3 days (t −3.20, 45 cases), against −0.75 % and −0.98 % for the other two thirds. It is outside this research's long-only box.
findings.F4: The book's gain is concentrated. Its 10 best days hold 79 % of the summed daily book returns, and its 10 worst days take back 57 %. Its 206 trades have a median net gain of +0.38 % and a 52 % win rate, and the top 5 trades make 41 % of the sum. This concentration, not a lack of edge, is what keeps Calmar at 0.20.
findings.F5: The other angles showed nothing that stands out after this many looks:

no_ideas: Across about fifteen variables and three horizons, the only long-side gradient in falling calm markets is the tested scaled 7-day rise itself (F1), and its look-alike, the range place, repeats it (F2). The strong patterns point short (F3, F5), outside the long-only box, and what limits the book is how concentrated its gains are (F4), which no new situation addresses.
